articles.title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Blueprints AI, a bootstrapped startup based in Santa Monica, developed software that produces code-compliant construction blueprints from a photo, PDF, or sketch.
articles.full_text:
Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings.

Al Dram was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him.

There was just one problem: The technology his idea required didn’t exist yet. “Then ChatGPT came along,” said Dram, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022.

His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible.

Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF.

Blueprints AI , which Dram officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 , a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.

During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Dram earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of PhD coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland.

He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Design-Build.

Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021.

Dram should have been satisfied.

He wasn’t. “I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.” Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt.

Dram and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day. “It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Dram.

He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.” Dram and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company.

Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer.

The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Dram’s design and construction firm, which is still in business.

Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 and $8,500 a month, depending on the plan.

Custom pricing for enterprises is also available.

The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade.

Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design.

Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration.

Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes.

Early customers are already using the second version, and Dram said it will become publicly available this week.

The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design.

The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders.

Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits.

The judgment stays human, they say.

Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software.

Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another.

The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project.

To learn more about Blueprints, catch hundreds of other startups, and learn from headliners like RJ Scaringe of Rivian and Amjad Masad of Replit, join us at TechCrunch Disrupt , kicking off Tuesday in downtown San Francisco.

articles.title: Honeyjar offers AI tools to improve PR and comms at every company
articles.summary: Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken. But could AI actually make things better?
articles.full_text:
Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant).

But could AI actually make things better?

Honeyjar , which will be attending this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt as part of the Startup Battlefield 200 , wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start.

The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise.

They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies.

Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm, Obvious Ventures .

As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an early-stage VC firm , where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch.

So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?” Honeyjar is her answer to that question.

It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities.

But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools. “Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building.

The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.” And it’s not just for founders.

Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.” “They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications.

It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.” Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals.

Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves.

She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.” When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek.

Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture.

That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists.

We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots.

When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish. “We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said.

And that’s also where judgment is key.

Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well. “For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.” In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage. “We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.” Topics AI , Media & Entertainment , Startup Battlefield 200 , Startups , TechCrunch Disrupt When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.full_text:
News AI Gadgets Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027.

The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. by Tom Warren Oct 12, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Microsoft Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services.

Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks.

Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie.

Image: Microsoft Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January .

Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Related Microsoft is finally making custom chips — and they’re all about AI Microsoft’s latest AI chip goes head-to-head with Amazon and Google Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains.

Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team.

Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models.

That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.title: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background
articles.summary: One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you'll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch, or record users' activity all the time and gather all possible context.
articles.full_text:
One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch, or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context.

There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously.

But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns.

Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar.

The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time.

The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and original design manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin.

Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs, and Apple Watch.

These apps act like meeting notetakers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day.

Meeting notetaking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems.

Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself.

The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data.

Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another. “The way we interact with intelligence is limited.

Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing.

That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” Mo, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch.

The company has ambitions to capture more information.

Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions.

Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar.

The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information.

Question of privacy Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user.

It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech.

Some meeting notetakers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversations and data without their consent.

Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Audio Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns .

Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default.

The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses.

Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users.

He classified this as an industry-wide problem. “We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture.

We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure].

We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said.

Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen.

The company is hiring for its go-to-market function and AI engineers for working on speech-recognition models.
